strengths: Strong engineering contribution: warm-started grow-shrink and Cholesky rank-one score updates yield substantial (>100x) speedups over BOSS while preserving theoretical guarantees (Markovianity in the sample limit), enabling order-based discrete search to scale to hundreds of nodes.

Comprehensive and honest empirical evaluation across many settings (ER, scale-free, several bnlearn real-world networks, path graphs, varying noise distributions, standardized/unstandardized data, DaO sampling), including reporting of cases where FLOP and all baselines fail (e.g., Pathfinder network, dense graphs with few samples), which strengthens the credibility of the claims.

The principled initial-order construction and ILS restart mechanism are simple, well-motivated additions that measurably improve accuracy, and the paper clearly demonstrates the run-time/accuracy trade-off by varying the ILS budget.

The work engages substantively with the ongoing debate about NP-hardness rhetoric and continuous relaxation methods, providing empirical evidence (BIC and DAGMA-loss comparisons) that discrete search is competitive with or superior to state-of-the-art continuous approaches like DAGMA.
Provides a usable Rust implementation with bindings to Python/R, aiding reproducibility, and includes clear proofs for the theoretical claims about correctness of the modified grow-shrink procedure.
weaknesses: The method and its theoretical guarantees are restricted to linear (Gaussian) additive noise models; no discussion or empirical evidence is given for how the approach might extend to nonlinear or discrete-variable settings, limiting generality.

Runtime comparisons are not fully controlled: FLOP is single-threaded Rust while comparison methods (BOSS, PC, GES via Tetrad) are multithreaded Java, and the paper explicitly acknowledges this is 'not apples-to-apples,' making it hard to disentangle algorithmic gains from implementation/engineering gains.

The core algorithmic contributions (warm-start grow-shrink, Cholesky updates, correlation-based initial order, ILS with reinsertion moves) are largely incremental engineering refinements on top of existing methods (BOSS/GRaSP, standard ILS metaheuristics, standard Cholesky update routines), rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea.

The paper does not compare against other recent methods explicitly mentioned as strong local-optima-escaping heuristics in the introduction (e.g., simulated annealing approaches of Kuipers et al., 2022), leaving the empirical comparison incomplete relative to the related work discussed.

The strong claim that 'optimizing the BIC is largely solved' on widely used linear benchmarks is somewhat overstated given the paper's own results showing failure on denser graphs, larger real-world networks (Pathfinder), and settings with fewer samples relative to graph density.

The practical guidance on selecting the ILS restart budget (a critical hyperparameter for the run-time/accuracy trade-off) is limited; in real applications without a known ground truth, it is unclear how a practitioner would choose this parameter or know when to stop.

strengths: Strong, extensive empirical evaluation across many settings (ER, SF, path, dense graphs, bnlearn networks, causalAssembly, Sachs, non-linear misspecified settings, varying sample sizes and parameters), with SHD, AID, and BIC-based analyses, lending good support to the central claims.

Concrete, well-motivated algorithmic contributions: warm-started non-greedy grow-shrink with a theoretical guarantee (Markov boundary correctness under warm start) and Cholesky rank-one update/downdate for local BIC scoring, yielding large empirical speedups over BOSS (>100x at 100 nodes) while scaling to 500 nodes.
The principled initial-order construction addressing weak long-range dependence in path-like structures is a useful, previously underdiscussed practical fix, with clear empirical benefit.

Honest and thorough discussion of failure modes: cases where the BIC optimum does not correspond to the true CPDAG (non-identifiability, faithfulness violations, non-linear misspecification), including the Pathfinder and Onion-method examples where more search leads to worse SHD despite better score, which is a valuable and rare kind of transparency.
Practical contribution of a fast, open-source Rust implementation (pip-installable), increasing potential impact and reproducibility.

The paper engages critically and substantively with the discrete-vs-continuous optimization debate in causal discovery, including a useful empirical point that FLOP-recovered graphs achieve lower DAGMA loss than DAGMA itself, questioning claimed optimization advantages of continuous relaxations.
weaknesses: Core algorithmic contribution is largely an engineering acceleration (warm-starts, Cholesky updates, principled initialization, ILS) layered on top of the pre-existing BOSS/order-search paradigm; the conceptual novelty relative to BOSS, GRaSP, and existing ILS use in causal discovery (Liu et al. 2023; Nazaret & Blei 2024) is comparatively modest.

The headline run-time comparisons against BOSS use a Java/multithreaded Tetrad implementation vs. a Rust/single-threaded FLOP implementation, which the authors themselves flag as not apples-to-apples; this weakens the strength of the speed claims and makes it hard to disentangle implementation-language effects from algorithmic gains.

No baseline comparison against more recent competitive order-based search methods explicitly cited as strong performers (e.g., Li et al. 2025), despite the paper's framing suggesting FLOP should be benchmarked against the state of the art in order-based local search, not only BOSS/PC/GES/DAGMA.

The method and theoretical guarantees are restricted to linear Gaussian ANMs with the BIC score; robustness experiments (non-linear, semi-synthetic, real data) show substantial performance degradation or score misspecification, somewhat undercutting the broader rhetorical claims in the abstract/discussion about discrete search being generally "reasonable" for causal discovery.

Some of the rhetorical framing (e.g., "recalibrating what is considered hard," dismissing NP-hardness concerns) is broad and could be seen as overreaching given the narrow linear-Gaussian, causally-sufficient setting under which the strong results hold.

Scalability, while improved over BOSS, is still limited to hundreds of variables under moderate time budgets; the practical relevance to real-world high-dimensional causal discovery problems (thousands of variables) remains unclear.

The ILS perturbation strategy (random swaps with k=ln p) and BIC penalty choice are essentially treated as fixed hyperparameters validated only via post-hoc plots (Appendix C.10) rather than a principled selection procedure, offering limited guidance for out-of-distribution problems where good defaults may not transfer.
